summary:
We've build an interactive map using electron, which can be used by Astronauts on laptops and tablets. It shows all the routes we made, boxwork clusters and 3 landing locations. Clicking a target flies the camera to it. The tool is aimed at crews choosing where to land and where to drive.

We propose three possible landing sites in Gale Crater and a set of routes to study boxwork formations. We also identified boxwork formations on the map and grouped them into clusters.

We also gave this mission a fun name: Curiosity's Gale
details:
We built a custom Mars map rendering engine, and it is fast. It combines several Mars layers and displays them at the same time. It takes all its imagery from NASA's Mars Trek tile services: Viking colour imagery, CTX and HiRISE mosaics of the Curiosity area, MOLA surface roughness and six TES mineral and dust maps — each with its own opacity and on/off switch.

We used Electron for the desktop build because it is reliable and cross-platform. Because the whole app is plain web code with no native dependencies, the same build also runs in a browser, and we publish it to GitHub Pages. Everything is written in TypeScript — including our own map rendering system.

It also draws routes and regions. They are extracted from Mars Trek as JSON geometry, which we use to show the boxwork clusters on the map. We found the clusters ourselves by looking at Mars Trek's HiRISE imagery of Curiosity's landing site — searching for them was the most enjoyable part of the project. We also read up on the topic, and added cluster A: it is quite pixelated, but we believe there is one more boxwork formation there.

We analysed the terrain around these formations and chose three candidate landing sites. We prefer the northernmost, site A. It lies near Curiosity's traverse, so its terrain is the best documented of the three. If Curiosity could drive through that ground, a crew could too — and crewed rovers cover in a day what Curiosity needs a month for.
